def: What an item was worth when it was damaged: the cost to replace it minus wear and age. Some policies pay ACV unless you have replacement cost cover.
The part of a home or renters policy that pays extra costs of living elsewhere, such as a hotel, rent and meals, while your home is repaired. Also called loss of use.
The person who inspects the damage and decides what the insurance company will pay. A staff or independent adjuster works for the insurer; a public adjuster works for you.
link: Dealing with an insurance adjuster after a fire

def: A portable machine that pulls room air through a HEPA filter to catch soot, ash and dust during cleanup.
The industry standard for fire and smoke damage restoration, first published in 2025. It covers inspection, cleaning and odor control, but not reconstruction.
The powdery leftover from burned material. Ash from burned buildings can hold metals and other harmful residue, so it needs careful cleanup.
A mineral fiber once used in insulation, flooring, ceiling texture and siding. Fire and demolition can release fibers, so older materials should be tested before tear-out.
Covering broken windows, doors and wall openings with plywood after a fire to keep out weather, animals and intruders.
Wood or other material that has burned black on the surface. Deep char weakens framing and usually means the piece is replaced.
A fire inside a chimney flue, usually from built-up creosote. It can crack the flue and spread heat and smoke into walls and the attic.
Your belongings, as opposed to the building itself. Insurance usually lists them as personal property or Coverage C.
A tar-like residue that builds up inside chimneys and stovepipes when wood burns. It is very flammable and causes most chimney fires.
The summary page of an insurance policy. It lists your coverage limits, deductibles and the policy period.
The amount you pay toward a claim before insurance pays the rest.
The loss in an item's value from age and wear. Insurers subtract it to find actual cash value.
link: Dealing with an insurance adjuster after a fire

def: A rubber sponge, also called a soot sponge, that lifts dry soot from walls and ceilings without water.
link: How to clean soot off walls

def: Powdery soot from fast, hot fires that burn wood and paper. It is the easiest type to clean.
The part of a homeowners policy that pays to repair or rebuild the house and attached structures. Often called Coverage A.
Sealing a surface, such as burned framing, with a stain- and odor-blocking primer so leftover smell and stains stay locked in.
A state-backed insurer of last resort that sells basic fire coverage when private insurers decline a home.
FEMA aid that helps states fight wildfires that threaten to become major disasters. Each state page lists these declarations.
Black, oily soot from an oil furnace or boiler, often spread by a puff-back. It smears with water and needs solvent cleaning.
High-efficiency particulate air. HEPA filters catch very fine particles such as soot, and are used in vacuums and air scrubbers during cleanup.
The most common homeowners policy form. It covers the house against all risks not excluded, and belongings against named perils such as fire and smoke.
The standard renters insurance form. It covers a tenant's belongings, liability and extra living costs, but not the building.
The standard condo owner policy. It covers belongings and the inside of the unit that the association's master policy leaves out.
A machine that uses UV light to make hydroxyl radicals, which break down odor molecules. It works slowly and is generally used with people present.
EPA rules for contractors who disturb painted surfaces in homes built before 1978, to keep lead dust from spreading.
The first stage of restoration: steps that stop damage from getting worse, such as board-up, water removal and drying.
Setting up fans and filters so a work area has lower air pressure than the rest of the building, which keeps soot and dust from drifting out.
Insurance that pays extra costs to bring a damaged home up to current building codes during repairs.
A machine that makes ozone gas to break down odors. The EPA warns ozone can damage the lungs, so it is used only in empty spaces.
Returning cleaned belongings to the home after repairs, checked against the pack-out inventory.
Inventorying, packing and moving belongings out of a damaged home so they can be cleaned and stored during repairs.
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons: chemicals formed when things burn incompletely. They are found in soot and smoke.
Fine particles 2.5 micrometers across or smaller, found in smoke. The EPA says they pose the greatest health risk among particles.
Testing a small hidden spot before cleaning a surface, to pick a method that removes soot without causing damage.
link: How to clean soot off walls

def: A signed, sworn statement of what was lost and its value, which some insurers require within a set time after a claim.
link: Dealing with an insurance adjuster after a fire

def: A thin yellowish film left when food burns. It is hard to see but has a strong, lasting smell.
An adjuster you hire, for a percentage of the claim, to prepare and negotiate your claim with the insurer. Most states license them.
link: Dealing with an insurance adjuster after a fire

def: A misfire in an oil furnace or boiler that blows oily soot through the ducts and into the house.
Insurance that pays what it costs to repair or replace damaged property with new, without subtracting depreciation. Often paid in two parts.
Covering roof holes and burned roofing with heavy tarps fastened to battens until permanent repairs.
The written, line-by-line list of repairs and cleaning a job needs. You and the adjuster use it to agree on what will be done.
Staining, residue, odor and corrosion left by smoke on surfaces and belongings, even far from the flames.
Fine black or brown powder left when something burns without enough oxygen. It is mostly carbon, mixed with chemicals from what burned.
A portable heater. Space heaters placed too close to beds, curtains or furniture are a common cause of winter house fires.
link: What to do after a house fire

def: A fire in or on a building, as opposed to a vehicle or wildland fire.
When your insurer pays you and then seeks repayment from the person or company that caused the loss.
Heating a deodorizer into a fine fog that travels like smoke into cracks and fabrics to neutralize odor. Done in empty spaces.
A strong cleaner used to wash soot and smoke from walls and some fabrics. It is caustic, so wear gloves.
link: How to clean soot off walls

def: Sticky, smeary soot from smoldering plastics, rubber and foam. It needs degreasers rather than dry sponges.
Areas where homes are built next to or among wildland vegetation, where wildfires can reach neighborhoods.
The lingering smell from smoke particles that settle into porous materials. It returns with heat and humidity until the source is cleaned or sealed.
link: How to get smoke smell out of a house

def: Cleaning hard items in a tank of liquid where sound waves shake residue loose, used for dishes, metal and small items.
